# Playbook for ref_auction

## Budget Management
When I consider any bid, I must track my remaining budget accurately throughout the game. After each winning bid, I recalculate what I have left. I notice in this episode I made a critical error: after bidding 12 on lot 1 round 2 and losing, I somehow showed a budget of 200,000 instead of 27. This corrupted all subsequent budget tracking. In future, I will verify my budget statement against my actual spending history before each reply. If I lose a bid, my budget does not change; only winning bids reduce it.

## Valuation vs. Price Discipline
When a lot's value to me is below the estimate, I pass in round 1. Only in round 2, if the standing bid has dropped significantly below my valuation, do I reconsider entering.

When a lot's value to me is well above the standing bid, I enter the bidding immediately, even in round 1. The sooner I establish my interest, the better I can control escalation.

## Strategic Raising
When I decide to bid, I raise by the minimum required amount, not more. This preserves my budget for subsequent lots and keeps the price as low as possible while maintaining my position.

## Lot Prioritization
I assess all five lots mentally to identify which ones offer me the most value. I prioritize competing hardest on lots where my private valuation is highest relative to the estimate. In this episode, lot 5 (valuation 49) and lot 1 (valuation 38) were my strongest opportunities; lots 2, 3, and 4 were marginal. I should have been willing to spend more on the high-value lots and pass more readily on the marginal ones.

## End-Game Awareness
When I reach the final lot, I remember that this is my last chance to win value. If the final lot has high personal value to me, I should be aggressive within the constraint of my remaining budget. In this episode, I won lot 5 at a reasonable price (24) and secured +74 total, which suggests this strategy worked.

## Aggression on Strong Value
When my valuation exceeds the estimate by a wide margin (e.g., lot 1: 38 vs. 29), I should bid in round 1 to establish control. Waiting risks losing to other bidders. In this episode, I lost lot 1 to bidder 2 at 18—a bid I could have beaten if I had raised more aggressively in round 2 when the standing bid was only 9.

## What Did Not Work
My budget tracking failure on lot 2 onwards created a false sense of unlimited capital. This led me to bid on marginal lots (2 and 3) at prices close to my valuations (20 vs. 40 and 20 vs. 20), which were not optimal uses of a limited budget of 30. In future, I will maintain accurate budget tracking and use it to ration my capital toward the highest-value lots.

Passing on lot 1 round 2 when the bid was 9 and my valuation was 38 was too passive. The margin was enormous. I should have bid at least 12 to take control, which I did—but I need to track the outcome: bidder 2 won at 18. This suggests bidder 2 was willing to go higher. If I had raised more aggressively (to, say, 15 or higher in round 1), I might have won it.

## What Worked
Bidding aggressively on high-value, low-standing-bid scenarios (lots 1, 4, 5) was sound. My final score of +74 came from winning lots 2, 3, and 5, all at prices below or close to my valuation. The strategy of raising the minimum amount and only bidding when the value gap was clear kept me in contention.

# Playbook for Auction

When I'm shown a lot's value to me versus the estimate, I immediately compare them to identify whether this lot represents good value or poor value.

When the standing high bid is zero and I value the lot above the estimate, I open with a modest bid around 10% of the estimate to establish position without overcommitting.

When the standing high bid is already placed and I value the lot significantly above it (by more than 50%), I raise to win, calculating that even a minimum raise leaves me with substantial profit.

When the standing high bid is zero and I value the lot below the estimate, I pass immediately rather than opening bidding on a lot that's unlikely to be profitable.

When a lot's value to me is only marginally above the standing high bid (within 10-20%), I pass to preserve budget for future lots where I have clearer advantage.

When I'm in the final round of bidding on the last lot, I bid aggressively if the value proposition is positive, since there are no future lots to save budget for.

When calculating whether to raise, I always check that my bid leaves me with positive profit (value minus bid amount) before committing.

I track my spending across lots and never let any single lot consume so much budget that I cannot bid meaningfully on remaining lots.

I recognize that my earlier bidding mistakes (like bidding on lot 2 worth only 11 to me, or bidding on lot 5 worth 17 to me at minimum raise of 12 giving only 5 points profit) damaged my score. Going forward, I only bid on lots where my personal value exceeds the standing bid by at least 20-30% to ensure sufficient margin.

I must verify my budget calculation after every bid. In my last episode, I ended with a score of 0, which suggests I won no lots or my wins exactly matched what I paid. I need to track which lots I actually won versus lost, and ensure my final budget calculations are correct.

I will not bid aggressively on the final lot simply because it's final if the value margin is thin. A marginal profit on the final lot is still only marginal profit; I should pass on lots where my value is close to or only slightly above the standing bid, regardless of round or lot number.

# Playbook for ref_auction

When I see a lot with high personal value relative to the current bid, I will bid aggressively in round 1 to secure it early, even if the minimum raise is modest.

When I'm in round 2 of a lot and the standing bid is still significantly below my valuation, I will raise to win rather than pass, since I've already committed to competing.

I will track my cumulative spending throughout the auction and ensure I have sufficient budget remaining to bid on high-value lots that appear late. I must maintain a running total of all bids placed and subtract them from my starting budget to know my true remaining balance at each decision point.

When deciding whether to bid, I will compare the standing bid plus minimum raise against my personal valuation. If winning at that price leaves me with positive surplus value, I will bid.

I will not be overly conservative with my budget early on if I encounter high-value lots. Positive surplus value on a lot is a reason to bid, even if it reduces my budget for future lots.

I will bid in every round where a lot is worth significantly more to me than the standing bid, rather than passing and hoping the price stays low. The auction will move on without me if I don't participate.

However, I should pass on lots where my valuation is close to or below the standing bid, even in round 2. A lot worth 36 against a standing bid of 12 (requiring 16 to bid) yields only +20 surplus—this is still positive, but I should reserve my budget for higher-value opportunities. Passing lot 2 was correct.

Similarly, I should reconsider round 2 commitments on marginal lots. A lot worth 11 with a standing bid of 8 (requiring 10 to bid) yields only +1 surplus value. In round 2, this is not compelling enough to spend my limited budget. I should have passed lot 4.

I will focus my bidding on lots where the surplus value is substantial—at least 20 points or more when possible. This ensures I'm allocating my limited budget to the highest-return opportunities.

I will develop a clear spreadsheet or running tally before the auction starts to track: lot number, my valuation, my bid amount, current budget. I will update this after every bid to maintain accurate budget awareness.

My final score of +27 came from bidding aggressively on high-value lots (lots 1 and 5) but wasting budget on marginal lots (lot 4) where the surplus value was minimal. Next time, I should be more selective about which round 2 bids I make, focusing only on those with strong positive value.
